raw_transcript:
Good morning everyone. Today we are examining what many jurists consider the heartbeat of the Indian Constitution: Article 21. Let us first read the text itself carefully. It is remarkably concise, just one sentence: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.'

Notice the deliberate choice of words. It does not say 'citizen', it says 'no person'—so Article 21 extends universally to citizens and foreign nationals alike. But more importantly, pay close attention to the phrase: 'except according to procedure established by law'.

Why did our constitutional framers choose this specific phrasing instead of the American concept of 'due process of law'? In our Constituent Assembly debates, constitutional advisor Sir B.N. Rau traveled to the United States and consulted Supreme Court Justice Felix Frankfurter. Frankfurter advised him that the 'due process' clause in the American Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments had led to severe judicial overreach during the Lochner era, where progressive labor laws were struck down by courts substituting their own economic philosophies for legislative will. Consequently, the Drafting Committee deliberately rejected 'due process' and adopted 'procedure established by law' from Article 31 of the Japanese Constitution of 1946.

Now, how was this interpreted initially by our Supreme Court? That brings us directly to the landmark case of A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras in 1950. A.K. Gopalan was a prominent communist leader detained under the Preventive Detention Act of 1950. He challenged his detention before the Supreme Court, arguing that the procedure under the Preventive Detention Act was completely unjust and violated his personal liberty.

The majority judgment, delivered by Chief Justice Kania, took an extremely literal and formalistic view. The Court held that 'procedure established by law' simply meant any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, regardless of whether that procedure was fair, just, or reasonable. If the Parliament passed a statute according to proper parliamentary rules, the Court could not question the substantive justice of the law.

Furthermore, Gopalan established what scholars call the 'Silo Theory' or the doctrine of mutual exclusivity. The Court held that the Fundamental Rights in Part III were distinct, water-tight compartments. Article 19 was one silo protecting specific civil liberties of citizens; Article 21 was a separate silo protecting personal liberty. The majority ruled that if a person was lawfully detained under Article 21, they could not invoke Article 19 freedoms like freedom of movement or speech.

For nearly three decades, this narrow, literalist doctrine held sway, leading to the low point of Indian constitutional jurisprudence during the Emergency in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla in 1976.

The watershed transformation finally occurred in 1978 in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India. Maneka Gandhi was a journalist whose passport was impounded by the central government under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act 'in the public interest', and the authorities refused to furnish any reasons for the impoundment.

She challenged the order, arguing that the right to travel abroad is an integral aspect of 'personal liberty' under Article 21, and that depriving her of her passport without giving her an opportunity to be heard violated natural justice.

The seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court delivered an epochal judgment that completely overturned Gopalan. Justice P.N. Bhagwati articulated that the Fundamental Rights are not isolated islands. Instead, there is an organic connection—what we now call the 'Golden Triangle'—between Article 14, Article 19, and Article 21.

Justice Bhagwati famously held that the procedure prescribed by law for depriving a person of life or liberty cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. It must satisfy the test of fairness, reasonableness, and natural justice under Article 14. In essence, the Supreme Court read the substantive requirements of American 'due process' right into the textual words 'procedure established by law'.

Through this interpretive revolution, Article 21 became the wellspring from which countless unenumerated rights later flowed—the right to clean environment, right to legal aid, right to speedy trial, and ultimately the fundamental right to privacy in the Puttaswamy judgment.

However, notice what remains bounded: Article 21 does not grant an absolute, unrestrained immunity. Where a valid statutory law exists, where the state follows a fair and non-arbitrary procedure, and where legitimate state interests are balanced, personal liberty may be constitutionally regulated. Next week we will examine how this doctrine applies to modern preventive detention and bail jurisprudence.
